newsitem.title: USA: AAA asks US for help in ending gasoline price rise.
newsitem.headline: AAA asks US for help in ending gasoline price rise.

text.p: The American Automobile Association (AAA), concerned sagging gasoline inventories could end up hitting motorists in their pocketbooks, is soliciting the government's help to protect consumers.
The AAA said it seeking the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) help to urge oil refiners to shore up their inventories to cool off prices, now 15 percent above last year.
"By keeping gasoline and oil inventories at such low levels, the traveling public is more vulnerable to the vagaries of the global market," AAA lobbyist William Berman said in a prepared statement.
In a letter sent last month to Energy Secretary Hazel O'Leary, AAA's President Robert Darbelnet said crude oil and gasoline stocks were at their lowest level since the 1973-1974 Arab oil embargo.
Gasoline stocks stood at 191.75 million barrels at the end of last week--nearly 10 million barrels below year-ago levels, according to the American Petroleum Institute, a trade group.

AAA's December price report showed the average price for self-serve regular gasoline at $1.29 a gallon, 17 cents higher than a year ago. Average monthly pump prices in 1996 were the highest since 1986.
"We are not suggesting the oil industry has purposefully manipulated prices but we are concerned that lower than normal inventories could put upward pressure on gasoline prices," Berman said.
The surge in gasoline prices began last spring amid low inventories following the long, harsh winter, which kept refineries focused on heating oil production at the expense of gasoline output.
The DOE has been aware of the low inventories and the threat of higher prices since last year, a DOE spokesman said, adding, however, the likelihood of intervention remained slim.
"We don't anticipate the government getting involved in the market," the spokesman said. "This is something the industry is best prepared to address."

Meanwhile, industry sources said oil refiners and marketers have in the last year kept stocks at lower levels, partly due to a new "just-in-time" inventory strategy aimed at freeing up money that had been tied to stock maintenance.

This is not the first time O'Leary has been asked to intervene on behalf of consumers. Last October, she met with oil industry leaders to discuss the connection between sharply higher home heating oil prices and the low stock levels.
And with the start of the peak gasoline usage season about six months away, a similar scenario is possible for gasoline.
"A price rise is very possible as we get closer to the driving season," said John Dosher, analyst at Houston-based Pace Consultants, Inc.
"The only way I could see them going down is if crude prices go down," Dosher said. referring to the way gasoline prices typically track those of crude oil.
-- Matt Daily, New York Energy Desk +1 212 859 1636
